paragraphs.text: Lesson 42, using vague language.
Martha is waiting for her teenage daughter, Rachel, to get home from a rock concert.
Rachel finally walks in the door at 12.30am.
Listen to their conversation and pay special attention to the freezes in blue.
Hi, honey. How was the show?
Pretty good. A bunch of my friends from school went. It was kind of crowded, though.
About how many people were there?
I don't know. I'd say 500 or so.
That's a good turnout. What time did it end?
That early? But it's half past midnight. Where have you been all this time?
Well, by the time we got out of the traffic jam in the parking lot, it was around 10.
Okay, and then what? Did you go to a friend's house or something like that?
We went to the diner to grab a bite to eat, but that Morris car got a flat tire, and no one had that thingamajig you used to lift up the car to change the tire.
Oh, uh, what you gonna call it? A tire jack.
Yeah, that thingy. So we had to call Kim's cousin who's good with cars and that kind of thing. Then we all went to Laura's house.
What'd you do there?
Just tongue out, you know, talking about school and boys and stuff.
Were there any boys at Laura's house?
Yes, tons of them.
What?
Chill out, Mom. I'm kidding. It was just me, Laura, Kim, and a couple of girls from Kim's class.
Oh, that's good. What are your plans for tomorrow?
Um, I have loads of homework, but it's supposed to be nice out, so I don't want to stay inside the whole day. If I finish early, I'll probably go for a jog in the park or whatever.
Alright, well, I'll be going out sometime around 11 tomorrow, so you're on your own for lunch. If you want, there's a bit of casserole left over from dinner.
Okay, good night, Mom.
Conversation vocabulary and phrases.
In spoken English, it's very common to use vague, not precise or exact expressions.
Quantities and qualities.
When estimating time, distance, number, or some other measurement, we often make a guess if we don't know or can't remember the exact number.
You can use around or about to show it's a guess. The more formal way is, approximately.
For example, it costs about $1,000, or it costs approximately $1,000.
Don't say this. It costs more or less $1,000. It doesn't sound natural to use more or less in this situation.
The most common ones are around and about. We drove around 10 miles. She's about 40 years old.
Another way to estimate quantity is to use odd and, or so, after the number. For example, there were 20 odd people in the meeting.
Odd is usually used directly after a number. He weighs 200 pounds or so.
To express a small quantity, you can say a couple of for countable nouns, meaning two to four objects, or a bit of for uncountable nouns.
For example, I brought a couple of T-shirts at the store. T-shirts are countable. You need to add a bit of salt to the soup. Salt is uncountable.
For food, you can use a dash of for spices and liquids, or a dollop of for soft substances. For example, there's a dash of paprika in this recipe.
To make this cocktail, take fruit juice and add a dash of tequila. I like to put a dollop of whipped cream on my hot chocolate.
On the opposite end of the spectrum, here are some vague expressions for large quantities.
Loads of and tons of. Both of these can be used for countable and uncountable nouns. For example, I ate tons of cookies at the party.
I drank tons of juice at the party. Cookies are countable and juice is uncountable, but we can use tons of for both.
The expressions, a bunch of, and quite a few, are used for countable nouns only. For example, there are a bunch of bookstores on that street.
I bought quite a few books yesterday. Finally, to describe qualities and sometimes time, we can add the suffix, ish.
For example, I leave the house at 6ish, maybe 630 if I'm running late. She has reddish brown hair, meaning brown with a little bit of red.
Two very common ways to say a little plus a quantity are sort of and kind of, which most people pronounce as sorta and kinda in informal spoken English.
For example, I'm sorta tired. These shoes are kinda ugly. The formal equivalents of these words are somewhat, or rather, placeholders.
Vague words are also used as placeholders, taking the place of the more specific word. We can use the vague word thing for objects, both physical and non-physical.
For example, how are things at work? Things have been going really well for me lately. What are those things on the table? Oh, those are computer parts. I was fixing my laptop. I'll put them away.
Here's the thing. Not everybody on the team is doing their part. In that sentence, here's the thing means here's the fact.

I'm not sure what we're going to do on our vacation, but I have a few things in mind. In that sentence, things refers to actions or ideas. We considered a lot of things before deciding to buy a house.
In that sentence, things refers to ideas or factors. We can also use the vague word stuff for plural and uncountable nouns.
Differently from the word thing or things, the word stuff is uncountable. Don't say stuffs. Here are some examples.
You like tomato juice? I think that stuff is disgusting. In this sentence, that stuff refers to tomato juice. A liquid or a substance.

When we moved to another city, I had to rent a truck to take all our stuff. In that sentence, stuff refers to physical objects, possessions. Sorry I'm so preoccupied. There's a lot of stressful stuff going on at my job right now.

In that sentence, stuff refers to situations. The informal words, what you might call it, thingamajig, and thingy are used for items for which you can't remember the name of the object, as you can see in the dialogue when Rachel doesn't know the name of the tirejack. If you are trying to remember someone else's name, you can use what's his name or what's her name until you remember it.

For example, I talked to that guy who works at the bank. What's his name? Randy Smith on Friday. Sentence, beginners, and enders. Finally, we have some sentence, beginners, and enders that help indicate that we are making a guess or being vague.

To make a guess, you can start your sentence with these phrases. It's difficult to say, but I think. I'd say, I'm not really sure, but I'd say, off the top of my head, I'd say, if I had to take a guess, I'd say, it's somewhere in the region of, or it's somewhere in the ballpark of.
This last phrase is used only for numbers. For example, it's somewhere in the ballpark of 100 miles.
In the dialogue, we also saw some examples of ending sentences in a way that leaves them vague or implies similar things.
Or whatever, and, or something. When Rachel says, I'll probably go for a jog in the park or whatever, meaning, or a similar activity.
And that kind of thing. When Rachel says, we had to call Kim's cousin, who's good with cars and that kind of thing. Meaning, and that type of topic or activity.
Or something like that. And, or something along those lines. When Martha asks, did you go to a friend's house or something like that? Meaning, or a similar activity of a similar type.
